claims.text: A combined high-throughput modulated DSC and in situ dilatometry protocol can accurately and efficiently characterize melting across representative high-entropy alloys.
DSC can be used to determine melting temperature.
The integrated protocol can measure fusion enthalpy and entropy across the HEA family.
The integrated protocol can determine volume change at melting and other liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
The integrated protocol will provide results comparable to or better than conventional separate techniques.
Calibration with reference materials ensures accurate latent-heat determination and baseline correction.
An inert atmosphere prevents oxidation during the melting measurements.
Testing variable heating rates can isolate heating-rate-dependent kinetic effects.
Melting manifests as an endothermic DSC peak.
Melting manifests as an abrupt volumetric expansion detectable by dilatometry.
Modulation and precise control of the heating profile deconvolve latent heat from background contributions.
Integration of the DSC endotherm yields the enthalpy of fusion.
Differentiation with respect to temperature, combined with latent heat, provides the entropy of fusion.
Simultaneous dilatometry records the volume change at the phase transition and links it to the thermochemical signature.
Fusion enthalpy and volume change on melting can be used in thermodynamic assessment and modeling.
The method will determine HEA melting temperatures with uncertainty on the order of a few percent, specifically about ±2% for high-quality samples.
Fusion enthalpy can be measured within approximately ±5% for high-quality HEA samples.
Volume change at melting will follow trends determined by HEA composition.
Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties will vary smoothly and continuously across the HEA family.

The approach applies to HEAs that remain single-phase solid solutions up to melting, while secondary phases, reactions, wide melting intervals, or extreme kinetic limitations can reduce its accuracy or efficiency.
